entries.label: Using hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent on a triangle with no right angle
entries.description: The student names the hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent sides of a triangle that has no right angle, as if those three names belonged to every triangle.

refutation.text_md: You are using the names hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent on a triangle that has no right angle. That is an easy step to take, because the names are used so often that they feel as if they belong to every triangle.
They don't. The book's rule is that these definitions only apply when you are working with a right-angled triangle.

Here is where it breaks down. The method starts with the right angle: the hypotenuse is the side directly opposite it, and the adjacent side is the side left over once the hypotenuse and the opposite side have been named. Picture a triangle with no right angle in any corner. Which side is directly opposite the right angle? There isn't one, so there is no hypotenuse to start from, and the other two names have nothing to be sorted against.

So begin every one of these questions by finding the right angle. If the triangle has one, name the hypotenuse directly across from it, then name the opposite side (directly across from $\theta$) and the adjacent side (the one left over). If there is no right angle, these three names do not apply to that triangle.

entries.label: Naming opposite and adjacent by where the side sits, not by the angle
entries.description: The student decides which side is opposite and which is adjacent from its position on the page (for example the flat bottom side is always adjacent and the upright side always opposite) instead of from the angle $\theta$ being used.
entries.signal: Opposite and adjacent are swapped whenever $\theta$ sits at the other end of the triangle from where the student expects it, while the hypotenuse is still right.

refutation.text_md: You are naming opposite and adjacent by where a side sits on the page, for example the flat bottom side as adjacent and the upright side as opposite. That fits many triangles, which is why it feels dependable, but these two names are not attached to any particular side.

The book says the opposite and adjacent sides depend on the angle we are looking at. The opposite side is the one directly across from $\theta$, so when $\theta$ is in a different corner, the opposite side is a different side.

Try it on two triangles. In the first, the right angle is at the bottom left and $\theta$ is in the bottom right corner: the upright side is opposite $\theta$ and the flat bottom side is adjacent. In the second, the right angle is at the bottom right and $\theta$ is at the top: now the flat bottom side is opposite $\theta$ and the upright side is adjacent. The two sides are in the same places in both triangles, but their names have swapped, because $\theta$ moved.

So keep $\theta$ in hand and label in this order. Find the right angle and name the hypotenuse directly across from it. Name the side directly across from $\theta$ as opposite. The side that is left, which forms $\theta$ along with the hypotenuse, is adjacent.

entries.label: Not checking that the hypotenuse is the longest side
entries.description: The student accepts a right-angled triangle whose marked hypotenuse is shorter than another side, because they treat the hypotenuse as simply the side opposite the right angle with no condition on its length.

refutation.text_md: You are treating the hypotenuse as just the side directly opposite the right angle, with any length at all. Finding that side is the right first step, but the hypotenuse has one more property that is easy to forget.
The hypotenuse is the longest side of a right-angled triangle. So whenever lengths are marked, the hypotenuse must be bigger than each of the other sides.

Test it on numbers. Suppose the side directly across from the right angle is marked $12$ and another side of the same triangle is marked $15$. That would make the hypotenuse shorter than a side of its own triangle, which cannot happen, so the diagram is wrong. Checking only that the $12$ is opposite the right angle would let this slip through.

Next time, find the right angle, find the hypotenuse across from it, then compare its length with the other sides. If any other side is bigger, the hypotenuse is too small and that is what is wrong with the diagram.

entries.label: Reads opposite and adjacent from the other angle
entries.description: The student names one angle but sorts the sides into opposite and adjacent as they stand for the other angle, so the two sides trade places and the ratio they write belongs to the other angle.

refutation.text_md: You kept the hypotenuse $q$ underneath, which is right, and you know that sine is opposite over hypotenuse. The slip is the top of the fraction: the opposite and adjacent sides depend on the angle you are looking at, and $p$ has been read from a different angle than the one named. $p$ is the side opposite $\hat{P}$, but this option is about $\hat{R}$.
The opposite side to an angle is the one directly opposite it. $p$ is directly opposite $\hat{P}$, but it is one of the sides that form $\hat{R}$, so from $\hat{R}$ it is the adjacent side.

From $\hat{R}$, the side directly opposite is $r$, so $\sin\hat{R}=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\dfrac{r}{q}$. Your $\dfrac{p}{q}$ is a real ratio, but it belongs to $\hat{P}$, where $p$ is opposite: $\sin\hat{P}=\dfrac{p}{q}$. For $\hat{R}$, $\dfrac{p}{q}$ is adjacent over hypotenuse, which is $\cos\hat{R}$.

Each time you change angle, redo the labelling: the opposite and adjacent sides switch places, and the hypotenuse stays the same. Pick the angle, find the side directly opposite it, find the remaining side that forms it, and only then write the ratio.

entries.label: Writes sine as opposite over adjacent
entries.description: The student finds the opposite and adjacent sides correctly but writes sine as the opposite side over the adjacent side, which is the tangent's pair of sides, so no hypotenuse appears in the answer.
entries.signal: A sine or cosine with no hypotenuse in it: a fraction of the opposite and adjacent sides only.

refutation.text_md: You found the right sides for $\hat{P}$: $p$ is the opposite side and $r$ is the adjacent side. The slip is which pair of sides goes with which ratio.

Each ratio has its own pair. Sine is opposite over hypotenuse, cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, and tangent is opposite over adjacent. $\dfrac{p}{r}$ is opposite over adjacent, so it is $\tan\hat{P}$, not $\sin\hat{P}$.
Sine always has the hypotenuse underneath, and here the hypotenuse is $q$. So $\sin\hat{P}=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\dfrac{p}{q}$.

Before you write a ratio, say which two sides its name uses, and check your fraction against that. If you are writing sine or cosine, the hypotenuse must be in the fraction; only the tangent leaves it out.

entries.label: Takes the ratio at the right angle
entries.description: The student writes a ratio of the two sides that are not the hypotenuse against the angle where those two sides meet, which is the right angle, instead of against one of the other two angles.
entries.signal: A ratio of the opposite and adjacent sides written as the tangent of the right angle itself.

refutation.text_md: You used the right kind of ratio for a tangent: opposite over adjacent is a ratio of the two sides that are not the hypotenuse, and $\dfrac{r}{p}$ is exactly that. What went wrong is the angle named: $\hat{Q}$ is where $p$ and $r$ meet, and it is the right angle.

Every question starts by finding the right angle, because the hypotenuse is always directly opposite it. The side directly opposite $\hat{Q}$ is $q$, the hypotenuse, and both $p$ and $r$ form $\hat{Q}$. So at $\hat{Q}$ the sides cannot be sorted into hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent the way the book does it.

Your ratio does belong to an angle, just a different one. $r$ is directly opposite $\hat{R}$ and $p$ is one of the sides that form $\hat{R}$, so $\dfrac{r}{p}=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}=\tan\hat{R}$.
Choose the angle first, from the two that are not the right angle. Then find the side directly opposite it and the remaining side that forms it, and write the ratio from there.

entries.label: Uses the ratios without checking for a right angle
entries.description: The student writes sine, cosine or tangent for a triangle without first checking that it has a right angle, as if the ratios worked on any triangle.

refutation.text_md: It is natural to carry the ratios over to any triangle: they are only fractions of sides, and every triangle has sides. The step that gets skipped is checking for the right angle first.

The ratios are built from the hypotenuse, the opposite side and the adjacent side. The hypotenuse is the side directly opposite the right angle, and the opposite and adjacent sides are then found from the angle you are looking at. In a triangle with no right angle, that first step has nothing to find.
The book warns about exactly this: always check that the triangle has a right angle before using the trigonometric ratios, otherwise the answer will be wrong.

So make it your first move every time. Find the right angle, then the hypotenuse directly opposite it, then label the opposite and adjacent sides for the angle you are looking at. If there is no right angle, sine, cosine and tangent as written here do not apply to that triangle.

entries.label: Calculator is not in degrees mode
entries.description: The student types the angle and presses the right key, but the calculator is set to an angle mode other than degrees, so every sin, cos and tan value comes out wrong even though the keystrokes were correct.
entries.signal: A value that disagrees with the degrees answer: for example $\sin38^{\circ}$ showing about $0.30$ instead of $0.62$, $\sin90^{\circ}$ showing about $0.89$ instead of $1$, or $\tan65^{\circ}$ coming out negative (about $-1.47$) instead of $2.14$.

refutation.text_md: You pressed the right keys and typed the right angle, so the method is fine. The slip is in a setting you cannot see in the keystrokes: the calculator has to be in degrees mode, and if it is in a different angle mode it reads the $38$ in $\sin38^{\circ}$ as a different kind of angle.

The same keys then give a different number. In degrees mode, $\sin38^{\circ}=0.615661...$, which rounds to $0.62$. In the wrong mode the very same keys give about $0.30$. Both are 'what the calculator said', but only one of them is $\sin38^{\circ}$.

You can catch this with a quick test before you start. The working for $\frac{2}{3}\sin90^{\circ}$ uses $\sin90^{\circ}=1$. If your calculator does not show exactly $1$ for $\sin90^{\circ}$, it is not in degrees mode. A sign that does not look right is a second warning: $\tan65^{\circ}$ should be positive, $2.1445069...$, not negative.

Before any question, check that the display shows degrees mode, and switch it if it does not. The steps for changing the mode differ a little from one calculator to another, so use the mode or setup key on yours. Then test with $\sin90^{\circ}$, and only after you get $1$ type in the question and round to $2$ decimal places.

entries.label: Looking for a cosec, sec or cot key
entries.description: The student searches the calculator for a cosec, sec or cot key, or tries to key one in directly, instead of first writing the ratio as 1 divided by sin, cos or tan.

refutation.text_md: It is natural to go looking for a cosec, sec or cot key: they are ratios of an angle just like sin, cos and tan, so you expect them to sit beside those keys. You are right about what they are. The catch is only in how you enter them.

On a calculator, the only way to get cosec, sec or cot is to convert it first into sin, cos or tan. That works because each reciprocal ratio is 1 divided by one of those three, with the same angle: cosec goes with sin, sec goes with cos, and cot goes with tan.

So nothing is lost. For example, $\sec65^{\circ}=\frac{1}{\cos65^{\circ}}=\text{2.36620...}\approx\text{2.37}$. Likewise $\text{cosec}140^{\circ}=\frac{1}{\sin140^{\circ}}=\text{1.555724...}\approx\text{1.56}$. The calculator only ever has to do a $1\div$ calculation with a key it already has.

When a reciprocal ratio sits inside a longer expression, convert just that part and leave the rest as it is: $\tan35^{\circ}+\cot35^{\circ}=\text{0.7002...}+\frac{1}{\tan35^{\circ}}=\text{0.7002...}+\text{1.4281...}\approx\text{2.13}$.
Next time you see cosec, sec or cot: write it as 1 over sin, cos or tan of the same angle, key that in, and round to 2 decimal places only at the end.

entries.label: Shares the function out over the angle
entries.description: The student treats cos like a number that can be shared out, so they accept cos(x+y) = cos x + cos y, or cos 2y = cos y + cos y, without working out both sides.
entries.signal: Says "true" for a statement whose left hand side applies cos to a sum or multiple of angles while the right hand side applies cos to each angle separately.

refutation.text_md: You're treating $\cos$ like a number that can be shared out, so $\cos(39^{\circ}+21^{\circ})$ becomes $\cos 39^{\circ}+\cos 21^{\circ}$, and $\cos 2y$ becomes $\cos y+\cos y$. Sharing out works for something like $3(a+b)$, so it is a natural thing to try, and you are right that $\cos x+2\cos x$ really is $3\cos x$. The catch is what the angle is doing inside the brackets.

Test it the way the question asks: work out each side on your calculator. Left hand side: $\cos(39^{\circ}+21^{\circ})=\cos 60^{\circ}\approx 0.5$. Right hand side: $\cos 39^{\circ}+\cos 21^{\circ}\approx 1.71$. The two sides are not equal, so the statement is false.

The same thing happens with $y=21^{\circ}$. Left hand side: $\cos 2y=\cos 42^{\circ}\approx 0.74$. Right hand side: $\cos y+\cos y=\cos 21^{\circ}+\cos 21^{\circ}\approx 1.867$. Doubling the angle is not the same as doubling the cosine, so this statement is false too.

The reason is that $\cos$ is taken of the whole angle as one number. The angle inside is worked out first ($39^{\circ}+21^{\circ}=60^{\circ}$, or $2\times 21^{\circ}=42^{\circ}$) and only then do you take the cosine. In $\cos x+2\cos x$ every term is the cosine of the same angle $x$, so you are just adding 1 lot and 2 lots of one number, and that is why it does equal $3\cos x$.

Next time, work out the left hand side and the right hand side separately on your calculator, with the whole angle inside the brackets, and then compare them. If they are different, the statement is false.

entries.label: Writes the fraction the wrong way up
entries.description: The student has the right two numbers for the angle but puts them the wrong way round in the fraction, so $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ becomes $\sqrt{2}$ or $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ becomes $\sqrt{3}$.
entries.signal: The answer is the correct value turned upside down: $\sqrt{2}$ for $\sin 45^{\circ}$ or $\cos 45^{\circ}$, $\sqrt{3}$ for $\tan 30^{\circ}$, or $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ for $\tan 60^{\circ}$.

refutation.text_md: You have the right two numbers for this angle; they are just the wrong way up in the fraction, so the answer comes out turned upside down.

Sin and cos put the hypotenuse underneath. In the right-angled triangle with two equal sides of 1, the hypotenuse is $\sqrt{2}$, so $\sin 45^{\circ}=\cos 45^{\circ}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$. Writing $\sqrt{2}$ on top is hypotenuse over a side, which is not what sin or cos mean.

Tan is opposite over adjacent. In the right-angled triangle with sides 1, $\sqrt{3}$ and 2, the side opposite $30^{\circ}$ is 1 and the side adjacent to it is $\sqrt{3}$, so $\tan 30^{\circ}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$. Put $\sqrt{3}$ on top and you have written $\tan 60^{\circ}$, where the opposite side is $\sqrt{3}$ and the adjacent side is 1.
Before you pick an answer, say the ratio in words (for example 'opposite over adjacent'), name those two sides for your angle, and put the side named first on top.

entries.label: Gives the value of a different ratio of the same angle
entries.description: The student picks a genuine special-angle value for the angle asked, but it is the value of another ratio: a sin or cos value for a tan question, the tan value for a sin or cos at $45^{\circ}$, or the sin and cos values swapped at $60^{\circ}$.
entries.signal: The answer is a value that belongs to the same angle's other ratio: $\frac{1}{2}$ or $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ for $\tan 30^{\circ}$, $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ for $\tan 60^{\circ}$, 1 for $\sin 45^{\circ}$ or $\cos 45^{\circ}$, or $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ or $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{1}$ for $\cos 60^{\circ}$.

refutation.text_md: You picked a value that really is a special-angle value for this angle, but it belongs to a different ratio. Sin, cos and tan of one angle come from the same triangle, yet each one divides a different pair of sides, so each gives a different number.

Sin is opposite over hypotenuse, cos is adjacent over hypotenuse, and tan is opposite over adjacent. Only tan leaves the hypotenuse out, so sin and cos always have the hypotenuse underneath and tan never does.

Take the right-angled triangle with sides 1, $\sqrt{3}$ and 2, where 2 is the hypotenuse. For $30^{\circ}$ the opposite side is 1 and the adjacent side is $\sqrt{3}$, so $\sin 30^{\circ}=\frac{1}{2}$, $\cos 30^{\circ}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $\tan 30^{\circ}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$. The fractions with 2 underneath are sin and cos, so they cannot be the answer for tan.

At $60^{\circ}$ the opposite and adjacent sides swap over: the opposite side is $\sqrt{3}$ and the adjacent side is 1. So $\sin 60^{\circ}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, $\cos 60^{\circ}=\frac{1}{2}$ and $\tan 60^{\circ}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{1}$.
At $45^{\circ}$ the two sides next to the right angle are both 1 and the hypotenuse is $\sqrt{2}$. So $\tan 45^{\circ}=\frac{1}{1}=1$, but $\sin 45^{\circ}=\cos 45^{\circ}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.
Before you choose, write which two sides your ratio uses, find those two sides for your angle, and put one over the other. Then check: a sin or cos has the hypotenuse underneath, and a tan does not.

entries.label: Uses a value from the other triangle
entries.description: The student takes a number from the $30^{\circ}$ and $60^{\circ}$ triangle for a $45^{\circ}$ angle, or from the $45^{\circ}$ triangle for a $30^{\circ}$ or $60^{\circ}$ angle.
entries.signal: The answer has $\sqrt{3}$ or a 2 in a $45^{\circ}$ value (for example $\frac{1}{2}$ or $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ for $\cos 45^{\circ}$), or $\sqrt{2}$ in a $30^{\circ}$ or $60^{\circ}$ value (for example $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ for $\tan 30^{\circ}$), or 1 for $\tan 30^{\circ}$ or $\tan 60^{\circ}$.

refutation.text_md: You used a real special-angle value, but from the wrong triangle. The special angles come from two different right-angled triangles, and each angle belongs to only one of them.

The $45^{\circ}$ triangle has two equal sides of 1 and a hypotenuse of $\sqrt{2}$. Its only numbers are 1 and $\sqrt{2}$, so a $45^{\circ}$ value never has $\sqrt{3}$ or a 2 in it. For example, $\cos 45^{\circ}$ is adjacent over hypotenuse, which is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.

The $30^{\circ}$ and $60^{\circ}$ triangle has sides 1, $\sqrt{3}$ and 2. Its only numbers are 1, $\sqrt{3}$ and 2, so a $30^{\circ}$ or $60^{\circ}$ value never has $\sqrt{2}$ in it. For example, $\tan 30^{\circ}$ is opposite over adjacent, which is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$.

Here is one more check. $\tan 45^{\circ}=\frac{1}{1}$ belongs to the $45^{\circ}$ triangle, because only there are the two sides next to the right angle equal. In the other triangle those two sides are 1 and $\sqrt{3}$, so $\tan 30^{\circ}$ and $\tan 60^{\circ}$ are never 1.

So start from the angle. $45^{\circ}$ means the triangle with sides 1, 1 and $\sqrt{2}$; $30^{\circ}$ or $60^{\circ}$ means the triangle with sides 1, $\sqrt{3}$ and 2. Then read your ratio from that triangle only.

entries.label: Reaches for the calculator instead of the surd value
entries.description: The student gets a decimal from the calculator for a sin, cos or tan of $30^{\circ}$, $45^{\circ}$ or $60^{\circ}$ and doubts that the surd form can be the same number, or gives the decimal as the answer.

refutation.text_md: Your calculator is not wrong, and neither is the surd: they are the same number written two ways. The calculator shows a decimal that fits its display, while a surd such as $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ is the exact value.

The book points out that for most angles a calculator is needed. $30^{\circ}$, $45^{\circ}$ and $60^{\circ}$ are the exception: they are the special angles, and you can write their values in surd form straight from a triangle, with no calculator.

For example, in the right-angled triangle with sides 1, $\sqrt{3}$ and 2, the side opposite $60^{\circ}$ is $\sqrt{3}$ and the hypotenuse is 2, so $\sin 60^{\circ}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. Key in $\sqrt{3}\div 2$ and compare it with your calculator's value of $\sin 60^{\circ}$: they should match.

So when a question says 'without using a calculator', or asks for surd form, write the surd: name the sides for your angle from the triangle and form the fraction. Then use the calculator afterwards only to check your answer.

entries.label: Names opposite and adjacent from the wrong angle
entries.description: The student labels the opposite and adjacent sides as seen from the other acute angle (or just by position on the page) instead of from the angle the question gives, so the ratio they write pairs the wrong sides.

refutation.text_md: You started by naming the three sides, which is exactly the right first move, and you know the three names. The slip is *where you named them from*: "opposite" and "adjacent" were read from the wrong angle, not from the angle the question gives you.

Only one side never moves: the hypotenuse is always the side opposite the right angle, whichever angle you are working with. The other two sides depend on the angle you are interested in. The opposite side is the one across from that angle, and the adjacent side is the remaining side.

Here is what goes wrong. Take a right-angled triangle with a $25^{\circ}$ angle, a side of length $7$ that is next to that angle (not the hypotenuse), and the hypotenuse $y$. If you read the $7$ as *opposite* (which it is from the other acute angle), you write $\sin25^{\circ}=\frac{7}{y}$ and get $y=\frac{7}{\sin25^{\circ}}\approx16.56$.

Now stand at the $25^{\circ}$ angle. The hypotenuse is $y$. The side across from the $25^{\circ}$ angle is the opposite side, so the side of length $7$ is the remaining side: it is the **adjacent** side. The ratio that uses adjacent and hypotenuse is $\cos25^{\circ}=\frac{7}{y}$, which gives $y=\frac{7}{\cos25^{\circ}}\approx7.72$, a different answer from $16.56$.

Next time, before you pick sin, cos or tan: mark the hypotenuse (opposite the right angle), then the side across from the given angle (opposite), then the side that is left (adjacent). Then choose the ratio that uses the side you want and the side you know.

entries.label: Does the wrong operation when rearranging for the unknown
entries.description: The student writes the correct ratio but gets the unknown on its own by the wrong operation: multiplying the known side by the ratio when the unknown is underneath, or dividing by the ratio when the unknown is on top.
entries.signal: The answer is the known length multiplied by the ratio when the unknown was in the denominator, or the known length divided by the ratio when the unknown was in the numerator.

refutation.text_md: You chose the right ratio and put the right numbers into it, which is the hard part. The slip comes in the rearranging: the step that gets $x$ on its own used the wrong operation, so $x$ was multiplied where it should be divided, or divided where it should be multiplied.

Look at what is being done to $x$ in the equation, then undo exactly that on both sides. In $\sin50^{\circ}=\frac{x}{100}$, $x$ is divided by $100$, so multiply both sides by $100$: $x=100\sin50^{\circ}\approx76.60$. Dividing instead gives $100\div\sin50^{\circ}\approx130.54$, which is not what the equation says.

When $x$ is underneath, as in $\cos25^{\circ}=\frac{7}{x}$, follow the book's two moves. Multiply both sides by $x$ to get $x\cos25^{\circ}=7$, then divide both sides by $\cos25^{\circ}$ to get $x=\frac{7}{\cos25^{\circ}}\approx7.72$. Writing $x=7\cos25^{\circ}$ instead would give $6.34$.

You can catch this by putting your answer back into the ratio. With $x=6.34$, $\frac{7}{6.34}\approx1.10$, but $\cos25^{\circ}\approx0.91$, so it does not fit. With $x=7.72$, $\frac{7}{7.72}\approx0.91$, which does.
Next time, before you reach for the calculator, ask "what is being done to $x$?", undo it on both sides, and then put your answer back into the ratio to check it.

entries.label: Presses the plain tan, sin or cos key on the ratio instead of its inverse
entries.description: After writing the ratio of the two known sides correctly, the student presses the plain tan, sin or cos key on that ratio, so the calculator works from angle to ratio instead of from ratio back to the angle.

refutation.text_md: You wrote the ratio of the sides correctly, and that is the hard part. The slip is at the calculator: the plain $\tan$, $\sin$ and $\cos$ keys go from an angle to a ratio. You already have the ratio and it is the angle you are looking for, so you need the key that goes the other way.

Take a right-angled triangle where the side opposite the angle $\theta$ is 50 and the side adjacent to it is 100. Then $\tan\theta=\frac{50}{100}=0.5$. The 0.5 is what tan gave from the unknown angle, so the angle is still the thing you have not found.

Pressing $\tan$ on 0.5 asks "what is the tangent of an angle of 0.5?", which is a different question from "which angle has a tangent of 0.5?". Only the second question is the one the triangle is asking.

The book describes the inverse tangent function as working backwards: it takes the ratio of the sides and gives the angle that resulted in that ratio. Inverse sine and inverse cosine do the same for their own ratios.

So after writing the ratio, press $\boxed{\text{SHIFT}}$ and then the key for the same function, and enter the ratio as a division. For $\tan\theta=\frac{50}{100}$ that is $\boxed{\text{SHIFT}}\enspace\boxed{\text{tan}}\enspace\boxed{50}\enspace\boxed{\div}\enspace\boxed{100}$, which gives 26.56505..., so $\theta\approx 26.6^{\circ}$. Written out, $\theta=\tan^{-1}\frac{50}{100}$.

entries.label: Writes "math error" instead of "no solution"
entries.description: After pressing inverse sine or inverse cosine and seeing the calculator's error message, the student writes the message down as the answer (or leaves it as the result) instead of recognising the ratio is out of range and stating that there is no solution.
entries.signal: The final answer is "math error" (or "error") rather than "There is no solution."

refutation.text_md: You rearranged correctly, keyed in the inverse function, and wrote down what the calculator showed. That is a natural thing to copy, and the rearranging was the hard part. The slip is in treating the message as your answer.

"Math error" is the calculator talking about itself, not telling you anything about the equation. What it is really saying is that you asked for an angle whose cosine (or sine) is a certain number, and no angle has that value.

Take $3\sec\alpha=1.4$. Converting to cosine and rearranging gives $\cos\alpha=\frac{3}{1.4}$. That number is greater than 1, and the largest value cosine can take is 1, so no angle $\alpha$ can have this cosine. The same is true for sine, which is why an error on either one points the same way.

So the error is not a keying slip to fix, and pressing the buttons again will give the same message. It is the calculator's way of showing that the ratio is out of range, and the equation has no solution.

Next time, when an inverse sine or inverse cosine gives an error, check that the number you keyed in is one sine or cosine cannot reach (here, greater than 1). Then write "There is no solution." as your final answer, not "math error".

entries.label: Using a negative coordinate as the length of a side
entries.description: The student takes a negative coordinate straight from the point and uses it as the length of a side in the tangent ratio, so the ratio and the angle come out negative.
entries.signal: A negative angle, or an angle of the right size with a minus sign in front of it.

refutation.text_md: You read a side of the triangle straight off the point's coordinates and put it into the tangent ratio, minus sign and all. Reading the sides from the coordinates is the right idea. The sign is the one thing to fix.

A coordinate tells you which side of an axis the point sits on and how far away it is. The minus sign only says "on the other side". A side of a triangle is a length, how far apart two points are, so it can never be negative. For a point at $(-12, 14)$ the horizontal side is $12$ units long, even though the coordinate is $-12$.

See what the minus sign does to the ratio. With the horizontal side $12$ and the vertical side $14-(-13)=27$, the book gets $\tan x=\frac{12}{27}$ and $x=23.96^{\circ}$. Using $-12$ gives $\frac{-12}{27}$, a negative tangent, and an angle with a minus sign: the right size, but not the angle in the triangle.

So before you use a coordinate as a side, ask how many units long that side is, and write that positive number. Draw the sketch, mark the right-angled triangle, write each side as a positive length, and then use the tangent ratio with those two lengths.

entries.label: Gives r a minus sign
entries.description: The student lets the position of the point decide the sign of r, writing r as negative when the point is left of the y-axis or below the x-axis, instead of keeping r positive.
entries.signal: Every ratio that has r in it comes out with the opposite sign to the correct one while tan is right, for example $\text{cosec}\beta=\frac{\sqrt{10}}{3}$ instead of $\frac{\sqrt{10}}{-3}$ for the point (1, -3).

refutation.text_md: You gave $r$ a minus sign because the point sits to the left of the $y$-axis or below the $x$-axis, as if $r$ travels with the coordinates. That is an understandable thought: $x$ and $y$ really do change sign from one quadrant to another, and you are right that the signs matter in these ratios.

But $r$ is not a coordinate. It is the distance from the origin $O$ to the point, the radius of the circle the point lies on, and a distance is never negative. As the book puts it, $r$ is positive because it is the radius of the circle. That is why the theorem of Pythagoras, $r^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2}$, is followed by the positive square root only.

See what the minus sign does with the point $(1, -3)$, where $x=1$, $y=-3$ and $r=\sqrt{10}$. With the correct $r$: $\cos\beta=\frac{x}{r}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}$ and $\text{cosec}\beta=\frac{r}{y}=\frac{\sqrt{10}}{-3}$. With $r=-\sqrt{10}$ you would get $\frac{1}{-\sqrt{10}}$ and $\frac{-\sqrt{10}}{-3}=\frac{\sqrt{10}}{3}$. Both signs are flipped, and the minus of $y$ has been cancelled by the minus you put on $r$.
Next time, find $r$ with $r^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2}$ and take the positive root. Then let only $x$ and $y$ carry their signs, read from where the point is, and substitute into the ratio you need.

entries.label: Pairs cosec with cos and sec with sin
entries.description: The student matches each reciprocal ratio to the ratio whose name it resembles, writing cosec as r over x and sec as r over y, instead of turning over the ratio it is the reciprocal of.
entries.signal: Cosec has x underneath and sec has y underneath, for example $\text{cosec}\theta=\frac{\sqrt{89}}{5}$ and $\sec\theta=\frac{\sqrt{89}}{8}$ for the point (5, 8).

refutation.text_md: You matched cosec with cos and sec with sin, going by the first letters of the names. It is an easy trap, because the names seem to point that way. You are right that the three reciprocal ratios are built from $x$, $y$ and $r$ in just the same way as the first three, so the pieces you are using are the right ones.
The letters in the name do not tell you which coordinate goes underneath. A reciprocal ratio is another ratio turned upside down, so what decides it is which ratio you are turning over.

Try it on the point $(5, 8)$, where $x=5$, $y=8$ and $r=\sqrt{89}$. The sine is $\sin\theta=\frac{y}{r}=\frac{8}{\sqrt{89}}$. Turn it over and you get $\text{cosec}\theta=\frac{r}{y}=\frac{\sqrt{89}}{8}$, with the $8$ underneath. The cosine is $\cos\theta=\frac{x}{r}=\frac{5}{\sqrt{89}}$, and turning that over gives $\sec\theta=\frac{r}{x}=\frac{\sqrt{89}}{5}$. So the $\frac{\sqrt{89}}{5}$ you wrote for cosec is really the secant, and your secant is really the cosecant.

Next time, write the first three ratios from the point: $\sin\theta=\frac{y}{r}$, $\cos\theta=\frac{x}{r}$, $\tan\theta=\frac{y}{x}$. Turn each over to get $\text{cosec}\theta=\frac{r}{y}$, $\sec\theta=\frac{r}{x}$, $\cot\theta=\frac{x}{y}$, then substitute your values.

entries.label: Putting the minus sign on r
entries.description: Given a negative ratio such as $\sin\theta=-\frac{15}{17}$, the student writes the minus sign on $r$ (so $r=-17$ and $y=15$) instead of on the coordinate it belongs to, and then divides by that negative $r$.

refutation.text_md: You read $\sin\theta=-\frac{15}{17}$ as $\frac{y}{r}$, which is right, and you noticed that the minus sign has to be written somewhere. You put it on the denominator, so you took $y=15$ and $r=-17$.

The catch is that $r$ is the hypotenuse, the distance from the origin to the point, so it is a length and is always positive. Only $x$ and $y$ change with the position of the point, so only they can be negative.

See what the wrong choice does. With $y=15$ and $r=-17$, the theorem of Pythagoras still gives $x^{2}=17^{2}-15^{2}=64$, so $x=\pm8$, and $\cos\theta<0$ makes you take $x=-8$. Then $\cos\theta=\frac{x}{r}=\frac{-8}{-17}=\frac{8}{17}$. That is positive, which contradicts the $\cos\theta<0$ in the question. Nothing looked wrong at the first step, so the slip only shows up in the answer.

The move that works: when a ratio is negative, give the minus sign to $x$ or $y$ and keep $r$ positive. Here $\frac{y}{r}=-\frac{15}{17}$ gives $y=-15$ and $r=17$. Pythagoras gives $x=\pm8$, and since the sine and the cosine are both negative the angle is in the third quadrant, so $x=-8$ and $\cos\theta=\frac{-8}{17}$.

entries.label: Not using the quadrant to choose the sign of the missing coordinate
entries.description: After the theorem of Pythagoras gives $x=\pm\ldots$ or $y=\pm\ldots$, the student keeps the positive root (or reads the signs of $x$ and $y$ from the ratio alone) instead of using the quadrant or range in the question to decide the sign.

refutation.text_md: You found the missing length with the theorem of Pythagoras, which is the right tool, and then kept the positive root, so the sign of $x$ or $y$ came from the square root. The trouble is that squaring throws the sign away, so Pythagoras alone cannot give it back.

Take $\sin\theta=0.4$ with $\theta$ obtuse. Then $\sin\theta=\frac{2}{5}=\frac{y}{r}$, so $y=2$ and $r=5$, and $x^{2}=5^{2}-2^{2}=21$. That gives $x=\pm\sqrt{21}$, because both $\sqrt{21}$ and $-\sqrt{21}$ square to $21$. Both are candidates.

If you keep $x=\sqrt{21}$ you get $\cos\theta=\frac{\sqrt{21}}{5}$, which is positive. But an obtuse angle is greater than $90^{\circ}$ and less than $180^{\circ}$, so it lies in the second quadrant, where $x$ is negative. The positive root cannot be the one, so $x=-\sqrt{21}$ and $\cos\theta=\frac{-\sqrt{21}}{5}$.

The reason is that $r$ is always positive but $x$ and $y$ change with the position of the point. The quadrant tells you the sign of each: in the second quadrant $x$ is negative, and in the third quadrant $x$ and $y$ are both negative.

The move that works: once Pythagoras gives a $\pm$, sketch the angle in the quadrant or range the question gives and keep the root with the sign that sketch shows. If a condition such as $\cos\theta<0$ leaves two quadrants, use the sign of the other value you were given to choose between them.
